idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines Channel fan-out: N worker coroutines receiving from one Channel
implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines - not the Kotlin stdlib - supplies the primitive: a Channel hands each element to exactly one of the coroutines receiving from it, so `repeat(n) { launch { for (m in channel) process(m) } }` is a complete competing-consumer pool and channel.close() is the end-of-stream marker. What replaces the classic dispatch structure is this fan-out contract; for cross-process or durable work the channel becomes a broker queue (Kafka consumer group, RabbitMQ with manual ack) and the coroutine workers wrap the client's receive loop. Channelled Flow operators (buffer, flatMapMerge) cover the streaming variant, at the cost of hiding the per-worker receive loop.
pitfalls: consumeEach in a worker cancels and consumes the shared channel on completion; fan-out requires a plain `for (x in channel)` loop.
Without a SupervisorJob (or per-message try/catch) one failing worker cancels its whole scope and stops the pool - in structured concurrency, siblings' failures propagate.
An unbounded capacity substitutes memory for backpressure; a small buffer surfaces overload as suspension, which is usually what you want.
